triage.reason: Seborrheic dermatitis is a common scalp complaint diagnosed clinically by history and skin exam, with recognizable distribution and appearance.

age.peak: bimodal: infants under 1 year and adults 20–50

demographics: Dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis in adults are more common in men than women
Cradle cap is very common in the first few months of life and usually clears by about 6–12 months
Scalp psoriasis affects both sexes about equally and often begins in the teens to 30s
Scalp ringworm is seen mostly in children

risk_factors.text: Family history of seborrheic dermatitis or dandruff
Close contact with pets or other children (for scalp ringworm)
Personal or family history of psoriasis

comorbidities: Seborrheic dermatitis of the face, ears, chest, or skin folds
family_history: Dandruff or seborrheic dermatitis in a parent or sibling
social_history: Frequent use of hair products, gels, or oils
Sharing hats, combs, or brushes with others
exposures: Other children at home or school with a similar scalp rash

chief_complaints.text: I have flakes in my hair and on my shoulders
My baby has crusty yellow patches on his head
I have red, scaly patches on my scalp that keep coming back

hpi.onset: Gradual, over weeks; cradle cap appears in the first few weeks to months of life
hpi.duration: Chronic and recurring in adults, with flares and remissions over months to years; cradle cap usually lasts a few months and resolves on its own
hpi.progression: Slow and fluctuating; flaking and itching come and go, often worse in winter or during stress, and improve with medicated shampoo but return when it is stopped
hpi.location: Scalp, especially the crown, hairline, and behind the ears; can extend to the eyebrows, eyelashes, sides of the nose, ears, chest, armpits, and groin
hpi.quality: Dry or greasy white-to-yellow flakes that shed onto hair and clothing; underlying skin may be red and mildly irritated
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; usually bothersome rather than painful
hpi.timing: Persistent, with flares and partial clearing
aggravating: Hair products that build up on the scalp

associated_symptoms.text: Redness or irritation of the scalp
Flaking or greasy scaling on the eyebrows, sides of the nose, or behind the ears
Crusting or scaling on the chest or in skin folds

pertinent_negatives: Well-defined bald patches with broken hairs
Severe pain or burning of the scalp
Pus-filled bumps or open sores on the scalp
New medicines known to trigger flaking

positives.text: Flaking or scaling of the scalp
Greasy or yellowish scale on the face, ears, or chest

negatives: Thick silvery plaques with sharp borders on the elbows or knees
Patchy hair loss with broken hairs

positives.text: Scaling behind the ears or in the ear canal

negatives: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour
New rash after starting a medicine

atypical.how_it_differs: Cradle cap presents as thick, greasy yellow or brown crusts on the scalp of an otherwise well baby; it is usually not itchy and the infant feeds and grows normally.
Seborrheic dermatitis can be much more extensive, inflamed, and resistant to usual shampoos, involving the face, chest, and skin folds.
Flaking may be drier and less greasy, and it can be harder to tell apart from dry scalp or psoriasis; response to treatment is often slower.

general.moderate: Well-appearing; may scratch at the scalp during the visit
general.severe: Well-appearing but visibly uncomfortable or embarrassed by visible flaking; no systemic illness
general.critical: Not applicable; this condition does not present critically ill

findings.maneuver: Part the hair and inspect the scalp under good light, including the crown, hairline, and behind the ears
findings.finding: White to yellow, dry or greasy flakes and scale on the scalp surface

findings.maneuver: Inspect the scalp skin after parting the hair
findings.finding: Mild to moderate redness of the underlying scalp skin

findings.maneuver: Inspect and gently scrape the scalp scale
findings.finding: Greasy, yellowish scale that clings to the scalp and hair shafts

findings.maneuver: Inspect the scalp of an infant
findings.finding: Thick, greasy yellow or brown crusts adherent to the scalp of an otherwise well infant

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyebrows, eyelashes, nasolabial folds, and external ears
findings.finding: Greasy scaling or redness in these sebaceous-rich areas

findings.maneuver: Inspect behind the ears and the ear canals
findings.finding: Scaling or redness behind the ears or in the ear canal

findings.maneuver: Inspect the chest, axillae, and groin folds
findings.finding: Greasy scaling or redness in skin folds

findings.maneuver: Inspect hair density and pull gently on several hair shafts
findings.finding: No patchy bald spots and no broken or easily plucked hairs

findings.maneuver: Inspect the elbows, knees, and extensor surfaces
Inspect the scalp for ring-shaped patches with central clearing
findings.finding: No annular scaly patch with broken hairs or black dots at the follicles

findings.maneuver: Inspect the scalp for pus-filled bumps or open sores
findings.finding: No pustules, crusted erosions, or purulent drainage

findings.maneuver: Palpate the cervical and occipital lymph nodes
findings.finding: No enlarged or tender lymph nodes

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the hands, wrists, and knees
findings.finding: No joint swelling, tenderness, or dactylitis

initial.test: Clinical scalp examination with hair parting under good light
initial.why: Diagnosis is clinical; identifies scale, redness, and distribution on the scalp, hairline, and behind the ears

initial.test: Skin examination of eyebrows, nasolabial folds, ears, chest, and skin folds
initial.why: Finds seborrheic involvement beyond the scalp and helps separate it from psoriasis

confirmatory.why: Confirms or excludes scalp ringworm when annular patches, broken hairs, or bald spots are seen
confirmatory.only_if: annular patch, broken hairs, or patchy hair loss suggests tinea capitis

supporting.test: Wood lamp examination of the scalp
supporting.why: May show characteristic fluorescence in some tinea capitis infections
supporting.only_if: tinea capitis is suspected and KOH is unavailable or nondiagnostic

supporting.test: Fungal culture of scalp scale and hair
supporting.why: Identifies the dermatophyte species when KOH is negative but suspicion remains
supporting.only_if: tinea capitis is suspected and KOH microscopy is negative

not_indicated.why: No role; seborrheic dermatitis and dandruff do not cause blood count abnormalities
No role; this is not a systemic inflammatory condition
No role; this is not a systemic inflammatory condition
Not routinely needed; only if other features suggest thyroid disease
Not routinely needed for an isolated scalp complaint
Not routine; consider only when seborrheic dermatitis is unusually extensive, inflamed, or resistant to treatment
Rarely needed; reserved for atypical cases that do not respond to treatment or mimic other conditions
Not needed for classic dandruff or cradle cap; order only when tinea capitis is suspected

not_indicated.test: Wood lamp examination of the scalp
not_indicated.why: Not needed for classic dandruff or cradle cap

not_indicated.test: Fungal culture of scalp scale and hair
not_indicated.why: Not needed for classic dandruff or cradle cap

decision_points: Diagnose dandruff and cradle cap clinically; no routine labs or imaging
If the scalp shows annular patches, broken hairs, or bald spots, evaluate for tinea capitis with KOH microscopy before starting a topical steroid
If thick silvery plaques with sharp borders are present on the scalp or extensor surfaces, consider scalp psoriasis
If seborrheic dermatitis is unusually extensive, inflamed, or resistant to treatment, consider HIV testing
Do not start a topical steroid on a suspected fungal scalp infection; it can worsen tinea capitis

differential.name: Scalp psoriasis
differential.why_considered: Scaly, itchy scalp patches are the most common look-alike; about half of people with psoriasis have scalp involvement.

history: Well-defined thick plaques rather than diffuse flaking
Family or personal history of psoriasis
Plaques on elbows, knees, or nails
Joint pain or morning stiffness
exam: Sharply demarcated plaques with silvery scale
Scale extends beyond the hairline onto the forehead or neck
Nail pitting or onycholysis
Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding when scale is lifted)
labs: No routine labs; consider ANA or RF only if psoriatic arthritis is suspected
imaging: Hand or foot radiographs if psoriatic arthritis is suspected

differential.name: Tinea capitis (scalp ringworm)
differential.why_considered: Fungal scalp infection causes itchy, scaly patches and is common in children; it can be mistaken for dandruff.
differential.trigger: Annular scaly patch, broken hairs, black dots at the follicles, or patchy hair loss

history: Scalp rash in a child
Close contact with pets or other children with a similar rash
Sharing hats, combs, or brushes
Patchy hair loss
exam: Annular patch with central clearing
Broken hairs or black dots at the follicles
Patchy alopecia
Cervical or occipital lymphadenopathy
labs: KOH microscopy of scalp scale and hair shows fungal elements
Fungal culture identifies the dermatophyte species
imaging: Wood lamp examination may show characteristic fluorescence in some infections

differential.name: Atopic dermatitis (eczema)
differential.why_considered: Eczema can affect the scalp and cause dry, itchy, scaly skin, especially in children.

history: Personal or family history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema)
Itching that is worse at night
Dry skin elsewhere on the body
exam: Ill-defined, dry, erythematous patches rather than greasy yellow scale
Flexural involvement (antecubital and popliteal fossae)
Lichenification from chronic scratching
labs: No routine labs; elevated IgE and eosinophils may be seen but are nonspecific

differential.name: Contact dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Irritant or allergic reaction to hair products, shampoos, or dyes can cause scalp redness, scaling, and itching.

history: Temporal relationship to a new hair product, shampoo, or dye
Burning or stinging rather than itching
Improvement when the product is stopped
exam: Erythema and scaling confined to areas of contact
Sharp borders corresponding to the application pattern
Possible vesiculation or oozing in acute cases
labs: Patch testing if the allergen is unclear

differential.name: Pediculosis capitis (head lice)
differential.why_considered: Head lice cause scalp itching and can be mistaken for dandruff because nits resemble flakes.

history: Intense itching, especially behind the ears and at the nape
Household members or classmates with similar itching
Nits that are firmly attached to hair shafts and do not flake off
exam: Live lice or nits cemented to hair shafts
Excoriations or secondary bacterial infection
Cervical lymphadenopathy
labs: No routine labs; diagnosis is by visual inspection

differential.name: Secondary bacterial infection (impetigo or folliculitis)
differential.why_considered: Scratching can break the skin and lead to pustules, crusting, and pain that may be mistaken for worsening seborrheic dermatitis.

history: Pain or tenderness rather than itching
Fever or malaise
Recent scratching or trauma
exam: Pustules, honey-colored crusts, or purulent drainage
Tender, enlarged lymph nodes
Warmth and marked erythema
labs: Bacterial culture of pus if severe or recurrent

severity.mild: Mild flaking of the scalp with little or no itching; no visible redness; responds to over-the-counter antidandruff shampoo.
severity.moderate: Noticeable flaking and itching with mild scalp redness; may involve the eyebrows, nasolabial folds, or behind the ears; requires prescription-strength shampoo or topical therapy.
severity.severe: Extensive, inflamed, and itchy scaling involving the scalp and multiple seborrheic areas (face, chest, skin folds); may be resistant to usual treatment and cause significant distress or embarrassment.
severity.critical: Not applicable; this condition does not present critically ill.

red_flags.finding: Annular scaly patch with broken hairs or black dots
red_flags.meaning: Suggests tinea capitis; do not treat with topical steroids alone
Suggests tinea capitis or another cause of alopecia; needs evaluation

red_flags.finding: Pustules, honey-colored crusts, or purulent drainage
red_flags.meaning: Suggests secondary bacterial infection; may need antibiotics
Suggests infection or another systemic process; not typical of seborrheic dermatitis

red_flags.finding: Unusually extensive, inflamed, or treatment-resistant seborrheic dermatitis
red_flags.meaning: Consider HIV infection or another immunodeficiency

complications.name: Hair shedding or temporary hair loss
Psychological distress or reduced quality of life

special_populations.differences: Cradle cap is common in the first few months of life, usually not itchy, and resolves by about 6–12 months; daily gentle washing with mild shampoo and soft brushing is usually enough, with prescription products for severe cases.
Seborrheic dermatitis can be much more extensive, inflamed, and resistant to usual treatment; consider HIV testing when it is unusually severe or refractory.
Flaking may be drier and less greasy, making it harder to distinguish from dry scalp or psoriasis; response to treatment may be slower.

key_questions.question: What does the flaking look like, and where on your scalp is it worst?
key_questions.looking_for: White to yellow, dry or greasy flakes on the crown, hairline, and behind the ears

key_questions.question: How long has this been going on, and does it come and go?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks; chronic course with flares and partial clearing

key_questions.question: Does your scalp itch, burn, or hurt?
key_questions.looking_for: Itching is common; pain or burning suggests another cause

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any patches of hair loss or broken hairs?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in dandruff; patchy loss or broken hairs suggests tinea capitis

key_questions.question: Have you used any antidandruff shampoos, and did they help?
key_questions.looking_for: Partial improvement with medicated shampoo that returns when stopped

key_questions.question: Do you have flaking or redness on your eyebrows, the sides of your nose, behind your ears, or on your chest?
Do you have thick, silvery, sharply bordered patches on your elbows, knees, or nails?
Any joint pain, swelling, or morning stiffness?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present raises concern for psoriatic arthritis

key_questions.question: Has anyone else at home or school had a similar scalp rash, or do you share hats or combs?
key_questions.looking_for: Close contacts with a similar rash or shared hair items suggests tinea capitis

key_questions.question: Do you have pets, or have you been around animals?
key_questions.looking_for: Exposure to pets raises concern for tinea capitis

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis, or psoriasis?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history supports seborrheic dermatitis or psoriasis

key_questions.question: Have you started any new medicines recently, such as lithium or interferon?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications that can trigger or worsen flaking

key_questions.question: Any fever, pus-filled bumps, or open sores on the scalp?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests secondary bacterial infection

key_questions.question: Have you had any unexplained weight loss, night sweats, or known immune problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; extensive or refractory seborrheic dermatitis raises concern for HIV

reasoning_points: Gradual onset of white to yellow, dry or greasy flakes on the scalp
Itching with mild scalp redness, worst on the crown, hairline, and behind the ears
Chronic, fluctuating course that improves with medicated shampoo and returns when it is stopped
Seborrheic involvement of other areas such as eyebrows, nasolabial folds, ears, chest, or skin folds
No patchy hair loss, broken hairs, or annular scaly patches
No thick silvery plaques on the scalp or extensor surfaces
No pustules, honey-colored crusts, fever, or lymphadenopathy
Diagnosis is clinical; no routine labs or imaging are needed

easy: Adult with classic white-to-yellow flakes on the crown and hairline
No hair loss and no other skin findings
medium: Flaking also involves the eyebrows, nasolabial folds, or behind the ears
Older adult with drier, less greasy scale that is harder to distinguish from dry scalp
Patient reports increased hair shedding during a flare but no bald patches
Symptoms worse in winter or during stress
hard: Infant with thick greasy yellow crusts on the scalp who is otherwise well (cradle cap)
Child with an annular scaly patch, broken hairs, or patchy hair loss suggesting tinea capitis
Patient with thick silvery plaques on the scalp and elbows suggesting scalp psoriasis
Unusually extensive, inflamed, or treatment-resistant seborrheic dermatitis raising concern for HIV
Scalp redness and scaling after starting a new hair product suggesting contact dermatitis
